title: His unpublished compositions and what makes a tune jazz
summary: La Rocca talks about his recently copyrighted numbers, a publisher, a song idea taken by others, and says any tune becomes jazz with the idiom applied.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: ...piece of sheet of sheet of sheet. And I had good luck on one of them. This last group. Yes. I put that with Charles H. Hanson Music Publishers. And he'll take more if I put them on tape. He's looking for original music of Nick LaRocca. And I couldn't tell you more on that. You've got some more. Oh yes. I've got about 40, 50 numbers. I have 25 of them I just had copyrighted in the last year. 25 copyrighted?

Within the last year? Within the last year. And I have 25 others that is not copyrighted. Then I have about 30 or 40 of them that has no copyright that I've had laying in the drawer for me. Many, many years. Many of them. I had men like Eugene West used to come to me for melodies. And I'd give them songs. And when they come out they were different. I'll show you in a pack right here. I give them a song and it was called Once In A While. And then they changed the title. And what you think they did, they took the title and put it on their song. And made my song, Summer In A Night. And this song went for a hit. And mine stood there, Summer In A Night.
I don't know. Do you have any pieces among the ones that you haven't published, which might be described as jazz pieces in the sense that Tiger Rag and pieces like that?

Yes, I've got others. I don't see it as good as Tiger Rag, but there's one in here that has a very good jazz number. And this Let's Jam It has plausibilities. Even this one that I put out as a popular number can be played in the same idiom that I would play it. And so on. There's nothing to it.
